A fee simple absolute, the fullest private ownership, which Alex may sell or will and which stays subject to government powers and lawful private limits.
An estate for years, a leasehold that gives Alex possession for a fixed term and leaves the freehold ownership with the grantor.

explanation: Alex received a fee simple absolute, the broadest private estate. Alex may sell it or leave it by will, and it does not end at Alex's death or on a condition. California presumes a grant passes a fee unless the instrument shows a lesser estate, and this deed states neither a life limit nor a condition. Government powers and valid private restrictions still apply.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a fee simple with a life estate. A life estate ends when the measuring life dies, while this deed gives Alex an inheritable estate with no life limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses fee simple absolute with a defeasible fee. A defeasible fee can be cut short if a stated condition is broken, and this deed states no condition.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a freehold with an estate for years. A leasehold gives possession for a term and is not the ownership estate this deed conveys.

prompt: In the sale of a single-family home, the parties have not agreed to include or exclude any item. Which item is personal property the seller may remove?

options.text: The dishwasher built into the cabinet run and connected to the kitchen water supply and the drain.
The garage-door motor bolted to the ceiling joists and wired into the building's opener circuit.
The mature orange trees that are still rooted in the side yard and have not been cut down, dug out, or taken off the land.
The freestanding refrigerator that plugs into a standard outlet and is not built into the cabinets or a fitted alcove.

explanation: The freestanding refrigerator is personal property. Real property is the land, things permanently attached to it, and the rights that go with ownership. The built-in dishwasher and the bolted opener are fixtures. Orange trees still in the ground are real property until they are severed. Because the parties did not agree to include the refrigerator, the seller may remove it.

distractorExplanations.a: Misclassifies a fixture as personal property. A dishwasher built into the cabinets and connected to the plumbing is annexed and adapted to the kitchen, so it is real property.
distractorExplanations.b: Misclassifies an attached fixture as personal property. A garage-door motor bolted to the joists and wired into the building is part of the real estate, unlike a freestanding appliance.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses fructus naturales with personal property. Perennial trees still growing in the ground are real property. Harvested fruit would be personal property only after severance.

prompt: An owner whose parcel touches a natural creek pumps water from that creek to irrigate crops on the same parcel and has never applied for an appropriation. Which right matches this use?

options.text: A riparian right, which comes from bordering the watercourse and allows reasonable use of the water on that same parcel.
An appropriative right, because pumping creek water onto the crops is a diversion for beneficial use even though the parcel borders the creek.
A license from downstream owners, because private use of creek water is personal permission rather than a right attached to the land.
A littoral right, the shoreline interest that belongs to an owner whose land borders a lake or the ocean.

explanation: This is a riparian use. A riparian right belongs to land that borders a natural watercourse and allows reasonable use of the water on that land. It comes from location, not from an appropriation permit. California also recognizes appropriative rights, based on diverting water for a beneficial use, with a state permit required for newer appropriations. These facts match the riparian system. They do not set a priority between the two systems.

distractorExplanations.b: Mislabels this bordering owner's on-parcel irrigation as an appropriative right. Appropriation is a separate system based on diverting water for beneficial use, and newer appropriations need a state permit. Touching the creek is the riparian clue.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a water right that attaches to riparian land with a license. A license is revocable personal permission. This owner’s use comes from bordering the creek.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses riparian rights with littoral rights. Littoral rights concern land bordering a lake or the ocean. A flowing creek is the riparian setting.

prompt: A mother deeds the family house to her son for his life and, at his death, to her daughter. The son moves in and writes a will leaving the house to a friend. Which interest does the son hold?

options.text: A fee simple absolute, because a deed that gives the son possession transfers the fullest estate the mother owned and lets him will it.
A life estate measured by his own life. He may possess the house, but the right ends at his death and the daughter takes the remainder.
An estate for years, because naming death as the end of possession works the same way as a lease that states a fixed calendar term.
A license the mother may revoke, because naming the daughter as a later taker means the son received permission rather than a present estate.

explanation: The son holds a life estate measured by his own life, and the daughter holds the remainder. He may possess and make ordinary use of the house, but the estate ends at his death, so his will cannot leave the fee to a friend. The daughter then owns the house. A fee simple would have let him devise the whole estate. This deed expressly limits him to his life.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a life estate with fee simple absolute. Fee simple can be left by will. This deed lasts only for the son’s life, so the will cannot pass the fee.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a life estate with an estate for years. A leasehold ends on a stated term. This estate ends when the son dies, which is a freehold measured by a life.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a life estate with a license. The son received a present estate by deed. A remainder in the daughter does not reduce that estate to revocable permission.

prompt: A buyer learns that the house is subject to a recorded driveway easement in favor of a neighbor and a lien for unpaid property taxes on that house. The owner can still transfer the fee. What are those two claims?

options.text: Life estates held by the neighbor and the tax collector, which would end when the seller dies and then fold into the buyer's title as what remains of the fee.
Present freehold estates that replace the fee, because a recorded easement or tax claim gives its holder an ownership share.
Encumbrances. The easement burdens use and the tax lien is a money charge, and transferring the fee does not by itself remove either one.
Personal licenses the buyer can end after the transfer, because neither a driveway right nor a tax claim binds a later owner.

explanation: Both claims are encumbrances, burdens on the property that are not ownership of the fee. The driveway easement is a non-money encumbrance because it limits use. The property-tax lien is a money encumbrance because it secures what is unpaid against that house. The owner can still transfer the fee, but the transfer does not erase those burdens. They are not estates and not revocable personal permission.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses encumbrances with life estates. A life estate is a possessory freehold measured by a life. An easement and a tax lien burden the property without giving the holders that estate.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a burden on title with ownership of the fee. The neighbor and the tax collector do not take the owner’s estate. Their claims sit on the property as encumbrances.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses recorded burdens with a license. A license is revocable personal permission. A recorded easement and a property-tax lien bind the property through a transfer of the fee.

prompt: Parcel North has no direct street frontage, and a recorded easement lets its owner cross Parcel South to reach the public road. The document says the right benefits Parcel North. What is that right?

options.text: A license the owner of Parcel South may revoke at will, because the crossing is personal permission and it ends when that owner withdraws the permission.
An easement in gross held by North’s current owner personally, which ends when that owner sells and does not follow Parcel North.
A specific lien against Parcel South securing a debt, because a recorded right to use a neighbor’s land is a money charge.
An easement appurtenant. Parcel North is the dominant tenement, Parcel South is the servient tenement, and the right runs with those parcels.

explanation: This is an easement appurtenant. It benefits Parcel North, the dominant tenement, and burdens Parcel South, the servient tenement. Because the recorded right benefits the parcel rather than a person alone, it runs with those lands. A later owner of North receives the benefit, and a later owner of South takes the burden. An easement in gross would benefit a person or a company, such as a utility, with no dominant parcel.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an easement appurtenant with a license. A license is revocable permission and is not an interest that runs with a dominant parcel. This right is recorded and benefits Parcel North.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an appurtenant easement with an easement in gross. An easement in gross benefits a person or entity, not a neighboring parcel, so it has no dominant tenement.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an easement with a specific lien. A lien secures payment of an obligation. This recorded right is a non-money use burden, not a charge for a debt.

prompt: A painter who was not paid records a mechanic’s lien against the one house the painter improved. The owner also holds a vacant lot the painter never worked on. How does that lien attach?

options.text: It is a specific lien, so it attaches to the improved house and does not by itself reach the owner’s separate vacant lot.
It is a general lien, so it reaches the owner’s other real estate as well, including the vacant lot the painter did not improve.
It is a homestead exemption, which protects equity in a dwelling and operates here as the painter’s recorded claim.
It is an easement appurtenant, giving the painter a permanent crossing right over the vacant lot as a dominant parcel.

explanation: A mechanic’s lien is a specific lien. It attaches to the property that was improved, here the house, and it does not reach the owner’s separate vacant lot. A general lien is broader. A judgment lien, for example, can attach to the debtor’s real property in the county where the abstract is recorded, not only to one improved parcel. The homestead exemption is not a lien. It protects some equity in a dwelling from certain creditors.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a specific lien with a general lien. A mechanic’s lien is limited to the improved property. A general lien can reach the debtor’s other real property, which this painter’s claim does not.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a lien with the homestead exemption. The exemption shields some home equity from certain creditors. It is not a charge the painter records against the house.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a mechanic’s lien with an easement appurtenant. The lien secures payment for work on the house. It does not create a dominant parcel or a right to cross the vacant lot.

prompt: Two sisters take title to a duplex as joint tenants with right of survivorship, in equal shares, under one deed. One sister dies and her will gives her half to a cousin. What happens to that half?

options.text: It passes to the cousin under the will, because a joint tenant can devise an undivided half at death the same way a tenant in common can.
It passes to the surviving sister by right of survivorship, and the will does not redirect the share joint tenancy sends to her.
The cousin and the survivor hold it as tenants in common, because death ends survivorship and opens the share to the will.
It passes to the cousin because the will's gift of her half severs the joint tenancy at death and leaves a share the will can give.

explanation: The surviving sister takes the decedent’s interest by right of survivorship. The deed expressly created a joint tenancy in equal shares under one instrument. At death, that interest passes to the survivor by operation of law and is not controlled by the will. A joint tenant who wanted the cousin to take would have had to sever the joint tenancy while alive, for example by a conveyance of that share. A will does not sever it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses joint tenancy with tenancy in common. A tenant in common may devise an undivided share. Joint-tenancy survivorship sends the decedent’s interest to the survivor instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Misstates the effect of death on joint tenancy. Death triggers survivorship. It does not convert the title into a tenancy in common with the devisee.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates how joint tenancy is severed. A will cannot sever it at death, because survivorship has already passed the interest. Severance must happen during life.

prompt: An irregular rural parcel is described by bearings and distances that start at an iron pipe, follow a creek and a fence, and return to that same pipe. What is the pipe’s role?

options.text: A township corner in the government rectangular survey, which locates land on a section grid measured from a base line and a principal meridian.
A lot corner in a lot-and-block description, which identifies the parcel by lot and block on a recorded subdivision map.
The point of beginning in a metes-and-bounds description, the monument where the courses start and where the boundary must close.
An assessor’s reference point that sets the property-tax bill and takes the place of a legal description in the deed.

explanation: The iron pipe is the point of beginning. Metes and bounds describes an irregular parcel by courses and distances from that point, and a valid description closes by returning to it. The creek and the fence are monuments along the boundary. The government survey instead uses sections, townships, and ranges. Lot and block cites a lot on a recorded tract map. An assessor’s parcel number is a tax identifier, not this legal description.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses metes and bounds with the government rectangular survey. That survey locates land by township, range, and section, not by walking courses from a pipe back to the same pipe.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses metes and bounds with lot and block. Lot and block identifies a parcel by lot and block on a recorded subdivision map, not by bearings and distances.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a legal description with an assessor’s parcel number. That number helps the tax office identify a parcel. It does not state the metes-and-bounds courses.

prompt: An owner glued custom mirrors to a bathroom wall and had them cut to the exact width of that wall, intending them to stay with the house. How do the fixture tests treat the mirrors?

options.text: They are fixtures and part of the real property, because they are attached, adapted to that bathroom, and were installed with the intent to stay.
They are personal property. Mirrors are decorative belongings, and fastening them with glue does not turn a bathroom fitting into part of the real estate.
They are trade fixtures, so this owner may remove them after the sale under the rule that lets a tenant take business equipment.
They are an easement in gross, because a visible improvement that serves the person who installed it is a personal right to use the land rather than part of the house.

explanation: The mirrors are fixtures and pass with the house unless the parties agree to exclude them. They are attached by glue, adapted because they were cut to that bathroom, and installed with the intent that they stay. Those tests point the same way, so the mirrors are real property. An agreement could classify an item differently, but nothing in these facts excludes them. A trade fixture is a business item a tenant may remove, which is a different party and a different purpose.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the mirrors as decorative personal property and stops once it notices they are not structural. Glue, a cut made to fit that wall, and the owner's intent that they stay are the fixture tests, and those tests make the mirrors real property.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an owner’s fixture with a trade fixture. Trade fixtures are business items installed by a tenant and may be removed in that setting. These mirrors were installed by the owner to stay.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a fixture with an easement in gross. An easement in gross is a right to use land held by a person or entity. The mirrors are physical parts of the real property.

prompt: Three coworkers take title to a cabin as tenants in common, with shares of one-half, one-quarter, and one-quarter. The half owner dies with a will leaving that share to a niece. Who takes the half?

options.text: The two surviving coworkers, in equal parts, because co-ownership carries a right of survivorship that overrides this will.
The niece, because a tenant in common has no right of survivorship and that undivided share passes by will.
The state by escheat, because a co-owner’s will cannot pass an undivided share while the other owners are alive.
The niece for her lifetime, while the coworkers hold a remainder that becomes a fee when the niece dies.

explanation: The niece takes the decedent’s undivided half. Tenants in common may hold unequal shares, and this form of co-ownership has no right of survivorship. The share passes by will. The surviving coworkers keep their own quarter shares. They do not absorb the half. Survivorship belongs to joint tenancy, and to community property only when the deed expressly adds it. The niece receives the same undivided half, not a life estate and not a physical slice of the cabin.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses tenancy in common with joint tenancy. Survivorship overrides a will in joint tenancy. Tenants in common have no survivorship, so the will controls the half.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a valid devise with escheat. Escheat sends property to the state when there is no will and no heir. This decedent left a will naming the niece.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the devised half with a life estate and remainder. The will passes the undivided fee share the decedent owned, not a lifetime right with a remainder in the coworkers.

prompt: A landowner orally allows a friend to park on a strip of the driveway. There is no writing, payment, or stated term, and the friend has made no improvements. What does the friend hold?

options.text: An easement appurtenant, because permission to park is a lasting right that benefits the friend as the holder of a dominant interest.
An easement in gross that the friend’s heirs can inherit, because spoken permission to use land is a transferable interest in that land.
A fee simple estate in the strip, because the landowner's permission to park transfers ownership of the ground the friend is allowed to use.
A license, which is revocable permission to use the strip and is not an interest in real property that runs with the land.

explanation: The friend holds a license. Bare spoken permission, with no writing, no payment, no term, and no improvements, is revocable permission to use land. It is not an interest in real property, it does not run with the land, and it does not pass to heirs. An easement, whether appurtenant or in gross, is an interest in land. Spoken permission does not create that interest. Because the owner allowed the use, it is also not the hostile use a prescriptive easement requires.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a license with an easement appurtenant. An appurtenant easement needs a dominant parcel and a servient parcel. The friend owns no neighboring land and received only permission.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a license with an easement in gross. An easement in gross is a real-property interest held by a person or entity. Oral parking permission does not create that interest or pass it to heirs.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses permitted use with a grant of fee simple. Parking on the strip does not transfer ownership. The landowner still holds the fee and may revoke the permission.

prompt: Spouses living in California buy a house during the marriage with wages earned while married, and the deed grants it to them as community property with no survivorship language. One spouse dies and wills that spouse’s share to an adult child. What is the result?

options.text: The will can pass the decedent’s one-half interest to the child, because this community-property vesting has no right of survivorship.
The survivor takes the whole house despite the will, because community property carries survivorship even when the deed does not use survivorship words.
The child takes nothing, because title in two spouses is a joint tenancy and a will cannot move a joint tenant’s share.
The share escheats to the state, because a will cannot leave community real estate to a child while the other spouse is alive.

explanation: The will passes the decedent’s half. Wages earned during marriage by spouses living in California are community property, and this deed vests the house that way. Each spouse owns an undivided half. Ordinary community property has no right of survivorship, so the decedent may leave that half to the child. The survivor keeps the other half, and the child and the survivor then hold as tenants in common. Survivorship would require an express community-property-with-right-of-survivorship vesting, or a joint tenancy. Neither was used.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses ordinary community property with community property with right of survivorship. Survivorship applies only when the deed expressly adds it. A deed that says community property leaves the decedent’s half subject to the will.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses community property with joint tenancy. Joint tenancy must be expressly declared and carries survivorship. This deed says community property and does not create a joint tenancy.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a valid devise of a community half with escheat. A spouse may will that spouse’s half, including to a child. Escheat applies when no will and no heir take the property.

prompt: A deed locates a parcel as the southwest quarter of the southeast quarter of Section 8, Township 4 South, Range 2 West, San Bernardino Base and Meridian. Which description system is the deed using?

options.text: Metes and bounds, which recites courses and distances that start at a monument and return to that point of beginning.
The government rectangular survey, which locates land by section, township, and range from a base line and a principal meridian.
Lot and block, which identifies a lot and block by reference to a recorded subdivision map and the map’s book and page.
An assessor’s parcel number, which is the tax office’s billing identifier and is not a legal description that locates the boundary.

explanation: The deed uses the government rectangular survey. It locates a quarter of a quarter inside a numbered section, in a township and range tied to the San Bernardino Base and Meridian. Metes and bounds would give directions and distances from a point of beginning. Lot and block would cite a lot and block on a tract map recorded at a book and page. An assessor’s parcel number is only a tax identifier and does not replace this legal description.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the rectangular survey with metes and bounds. Metes and bounds walks courses from a point of beginning. This deed uses a section, township, and range instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the rectangular survey with lot and block. Lot and block cites a lot on a recorded subdivision map. A section and township are not a lot and block call.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a government-survey legal description with an assessor’s parcel number. The parcel number is a tax identifier. This deed locates the land by section, township, and range.

prompt: A city limits new buildings on a street to two stories so fire equipment can operate. Owners keep title. The city files no condemnation case and offers no payment. Which power is the city using?

options.text: Eminent domain, because a height limit takes unused airspace and requires just compensation even though the owners keep their lots.
Escheat, because building height the ordinance does not allow passes to the state when no private owner is left to hold it.
Police power, because the city is regulating use for public safety, leaving title with the owners, without condemning the lots.
Taxation, because a use restriction is collected as a property tax and the height rule is a tax rather than a land-use regulation.

explanation: The city is using the police power, the authority to regulate land for the public health, safety, and general welfare. A two-story limit adopted so fire equipment can operate leaves title and possession with the owners. It is not a condemnation. Eminent domain is the separate power to take private property for a public use, and that power requires just compensation. Escheat and taxation do not describe a height limit. This ordinary use regulation is not itself a taking that must be paid for before it applies.

distractorExplanations.a: Mislabels police-power regulation as eminent domain. Eminent domain takes property for a public use and pays just compensation. A height limit that leaves the owners in possession is not that taking.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses police power with escheat. Escheat transfers title to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs. A height limit does not move title and does not depend on an owner’s death.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a land-use regulation with taxation. Taxation is the power to levy taxes, and unpaid property taxes can become a lien. A height limit regulates use. It is not a tax.

prompt: A sole owner dies without a will and with no known heirs. The estate process finds no person entitled to take the house. Where does title to the house go?

options.text: To the city by eminent domain, because an heirless house is treated as taken for public use and the city holds title through that taking.
It remains with the city under the police power, which regulates use and also keeps title when an owner dies.
To the tax collector through the power of taxation, because an unpaid-tax lien is how ownerless real estate is received.
To the state by escheat, the power used when a person dies leaving property and neither a will nor an heir to take it.

explanation: Title escheats to the state when a person dies leaving property and no will and no heir entitled to take it. Escheat is one of the four government powers over private land. Police power regulates use and does not transfer title at death. Eminent domain takes property for a public use and requires just compensation. Taxation levies taxes, and unpaid property taxes can become a lien. None of those three is how an heirless intestate estate passes.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses escheat with eminent domain. Eminent domain takes property for a public use and requires just compensation. It is not the result of dying without a will and without heirs.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses escheat with the police power. Police power regulates how land is used. It does not transfer title to the government because the owner died without heirs.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses escheat with taxation. Taxation is the power to levy taxes, and unpaid property taxes may become a lien. A tax lien is not the path for an heirless estate.

prompt: A subdivision’s recorded declaration bans backyard workshops. City zoning allows a workshop as an accessory use on the same lot. The buyer wants to build one. Which limit controls the workshop?

options.text: Zoning controls and the covenant drops out, because a city land-use ordinance displaces a private restriction that covers the same workshop use.
The ban is an easement in gross held by the city, so the planning department, rather than the other owners, enforces it.
The private ban still applies. Zoning that allows the workshop does not cancel a stricter recorded covenant, so the owner must follow both.
The covenant is void because it is stricter than the zoning map, and a private rule cannot limit a use the city has allowed.

explanation: Zoning and private restrictions can bind the same lot at the same time. Zoning is a public control under the police power. A recorded declaration is a private restriction, enforced by other owners or an association, when it is a valid covenant that runs with the lots. The city allows the workshop, but the covenant forbids it, so the owner cannot build while the covenant remains. A covenant that violates fair housing law would be unenforceable. A ban on workshops is a use limit, not that kind of clause.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates the relationship between zoning and covenants. A more permissive zoning rule does not cancel a stricter private restriction. The owner must comply with the public rule and the covenant.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a private covenant with an easement in gross held by the city. The declaration is a private use restriction. Zoning is the city’s separate public control, enforced by the city.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates when a covenant fails. A covenant is not void merely because it is stricter than zoning. Unlawful discriminatory restrictions are a different problem. This workshop ban can still be enforced.

prompt: A city withholds a building permit until the owner completes a fault study, because the lot is in a mapped earthquake fault zone, and it requires fire-resistant construction because the lot is in a high fire-hazard area. What is the city applying?

options.text: Eminent domain, because a required hazard study means the city is acquiring the lot and must pay just compensation before denying a permit.
A private covenant, because hazard-zone maps are deed restrictions among neighbors and are enforced by a homeowners association.
Escheat, because land in a mapped hazard area returns to the state and the owner must transfer the fee before building.
Environmental and natural-hazard rules as land-use controls, which can limit how a risky parcel is built on without the city taking title.

explanation: The city is applying environmental and natural-hazard land-use controls. A mapped earthquake fault zone can require a geologic study, and California’s Alquist-Priolo Earthquake Fault Zoning Act restricts buildings for human occupancy on active fault traces. A high fire-hazard area can require fire-resistant construction. These rules limit how the parcel is built on. They are an exercise of the police power aimed at a physical risk. The city is not taking title, so this is not eminent domain, a private covenant, or escheat.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses hazard regulation with eminent domain. Eminent domain acquires property for a public use and requires just compensation. Requiring a fault study and safer construction leaves title with the owner.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses public hazard-zone rules with a private covenant. Fault and fire maps are government land-use controls. They are not CC&Rs enforced by a homeowners association.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses hazard regulation with escheat. Escheat transfers title to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs. A hazard zone does not make the owner deed the fee to the state.

prompt: An informed buyer and an informed seller, neither one acting under pressure, would most probably agree on a price in an open market. What is that figure?

options.text: The assessed value the county uses when it calculates the property tax
The historical price this owner paid when acquiring the same house
The contractor's current bill to rebuild the house after a total loss
The market value of the property in a fair and competitive sale

explanation: Market value is the most probable price a property would bring in an open and competitive market when both parties are informed, typically motivated, and not acting under undue pressure. It is an opinion of worth under those conditions. The county's assessed value is a tax figure and often differs from what buyers will pay. The price the owner paid in the past, and the cost to rebuild, are not that probable price.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses market value with assessed value. The assessor's figure is used for property tax and can sit well above or below the price informed parties would agree on today.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses market value with a past transaction price. What this owner once paid is history, not the most probable price in the current open market.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses market value with cost. A contractor's bill to rebuild is a cost figure used in the cost approach, not the probable open-market price.

prompt: A buyer will not pay more for this house than for an equally desirable house offered in the same neighborhood. Which principle sets that ceiling?

options.text: Substitution, which caps price at the cost of an equal substitute
Contribution, which values a part by what it adds to the whole
Conformity, which ties value to similarity with surrounding homes
Anticipation, which bases value on expected benefits in the future

explanation: The principle of substitution says a prudent buyer will pay no more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute. That ceiling is why recent sales of similar houses, and the cost to produce a substitute, restrain price. Contribution measures one component, conformity looks at fit with the neighborhood, and anticipation looks at expected future benefits.

distractorExplanations.b: Names contribution, which prices a component by what it adds to the property. The ceiling set by an equally desirable house nearby is substitution.
distractorExplanations.c: Names conformity, which says value is highest when a property fits its surroundings. It does not set the ceiling at the price of a substitute.
distractorExplanations.d: Names anticipation, which derives value from benefits expected in the future. The buyer's limit here is the cost of a substitute available now.

prompt: A homeowner spends heavily on a new pool, but nearby resales show that the pool adds less than it cost. Which principle measures what the pool adds?

options.text: Substitution, the ceiling set by the price of a similar house
Contribution, the value a component adds rather than its cost
Conformity, the gain from matching the houses on the block
Change, the shift in prices as neighborhood conditions move

explanation: The principle of contribution says a component is worth what it adds to the value of the whole property, which may be more or less than its cost. A pool that buyers will not fully repay at resale contributes its market increment, not the owner's invoice. Substitution compares whole substitutes, conformity compares the property with its neighbors, and change describes markets moving over time.

distractorExplanations.a: Names substitution, the limit set by an equally desirable property. The gap between the pool's cost and the resale increment is contribution.
distractorExplanations.c: Names conformity, similarity with surrounding property. A pool worth less than it cost is a contribution problem even when the house otherwise fits the block.
distractorExplanations.d: Names the principle of change, which says values shift as conditions shift. It does not measure what one improvement adds to price.

prompt: Houses on this block reach their highest value when size and style are reasonably like the neighboring houses. Which principle explains that pattern?

options.text: Progression, a modest house gaining from better houses nearby
Regression, a superior house losing value near lesser houses
Conformity, the value peak when a house matches its surroundings
Contribution, the amount one feature adds to the property as a whole

explanation: The principle of conformity says a property reaches its maximum value when it is reasonably similar to surrounding properties in size, style, and use. Progression is the lift a lesser property can get from better neighbors, and regression is the drag on a superior property from lesser neighbors. Those are effects of a mismatch. Contribution prices a single component, not the fit with the block.

distractorExplanations.a: Names progression, the boost to a lower-valued house located among higher-valued ones. The stem states the value peak that comes from similarity, which is conformity.
distractorExplanations.b: Names regression, the loss a higher-valued house can suffer among lower-valued ones. That is a result of failing to conform, not the principle that similarity produces the highest value.
distractorExplanations.d: Names contribution, what one component adds to the whole. Neighborhood similarity, not a single feature's increment, is the pattern in the stem.

prompt: A comparable house that just sold has one more bathroom than the subject property. In the sales comparison approach, what should the appraiser do?

options.text: Add a bathroom adjustment to the comparable's sale price
Add a bathroom adjustment to the subject's value indication
Subtract a bathroom adjustment from the subject's value indication
Subtract a bathroom adjustment from the comparable's sale price

explanation: In the sales comparison approach the appraiser adjusts the comparable sales, not the subject, until each comparable matches the subject. This comparable is better by one bathroom, so the appraiser subtracts the market contribution of that bathroom from the comparable's sale price. Adding would fit a comparable that lacked a bathroom the subject has. The subject's indication is the result of the adjusted sales, not a number the appraiser nudges feature by feature.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the direction. An extra bathroom makes the comparable superior to the subject, so its sale price is reduced, not increased.
distractorExplanations.b: Adjusts the subject instead of the comparable. Sales comparison leaves the subject as the base and changes the comparable's sale price.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts from the wrong property. The extra bathroom belongs to the comparable, so the deduction comes off the comparable's sale price.

prompt: For a new special-purpose building with few similar sales, an appraiser adds land value to current construction cost and then subtracts depreciation. Which approach is that?

options.text: The cost approach, land value plus cost new minus depreciation
The sales comparison approach, adjusting prices of similar sales
The income approach, capitalizing net operating income into value
A gross rent multiplier, sale price divided by gross rent

explanation: The cost approach estimates value as land value plus the current cost of the improvements, minus depreciation. Depreciation in that subtraction can be physical, functional, or external. The approach is useful when similar sales are scarce, as with a new or special-purpose building. Sales comparison adjusts sale prices, the income approach capitalizes net operating income, and a gross rent multiplier relates sale price to gross rent.

distractorExplanations.b: Names sales comparison, which adjusts the prices of similar properties that sold. Adding land value to cost new and subtracting depreciation is the cost approach.
distractorExplanations.c: Names the income approach, which converts net operating income into value with a capitalization rate. Cost and depreciation are not that method.
distractorExplanations.d: Names the gross rent multiplier, sale price divided by gross rent. The work in the stem uses land value, construction cost, and depreciation.

prompt: The roof leaks, the exterior paint is peeling, and the water heater has worn out from years of ordinary use. Which depreciation is that loss?

options.text: Functional obsolescence from an outdated floor plan inside the house
Physical deterioration from wear, damage, and aging of the structure
External obsolescence from a condition lying outside the lot lines
Accounting depreciation claimed on the owner's income-tax return

explanation: Physical deterioration is loss in value from wear, tear, damage, or aging of the improvements themselves. A leaking roof, peeling paint, and a worn-out water heater are that kind of loss. The category stays physical whether the item is curable deferred maintenance or longer-lived wear. Functional obsolescence is a design problem, external obsolescence comes from outside the property, and a tax-return write-off is not appraisal depreciation.

distractorExplanations.a: Names functional obsolescence, a loss from layout or design such as a poor floor plan. Worn and damaged building parts are physical deterioration.
distractorExplanations.c: Names external obsolescence, a loss from outside the property lines. The defects in the stem are in the building itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses appraisal depreciation with an income-tax deduction. A schedule on a tax return does not classify a leaking roof for the cost approach.

prompt: A five-bedroom house has a single bathroom, and buyers discount the house for that outdated layout. Which depreciation is the discount?

options.text: Physical deterioration from wear on the bedrooms and the bathroom
External obsolescence from a use that changed on the next block
Functional obsolescence from a layout that misses current market taste
Curable physical loss, because one more bathroom would remove it

explanation: Functional obsolescence is a loss in value from the property's own design, layout, or utility, such as five bedrooms served by one bathroom. It may be curable when the cost to fix it is justified by the value added, or incurable when it is not. The category is functional either way. Wear is physical deterioration. A layout problem stays functional even when another bathroom would cure it. Off-site conditions are external obsolescence.

distractorExplanations.a: Names physical deterioration, wear and aging of the structure. The discount is for the bathroom count and layout, not for worn materials.
distractorExplanations.b: Names external obsolescence, a loss caused outside the property. The outdated bathroom layout is inside the house, so the loss is functional.
distractorExplanations.d: Calls the layout curable physical deterioration. Adding a bathroom may cure the obsolescence, but a design shortfall is functional whether or not the cure pays.

prompt: A busy freeway is built directly behind a house that had been on a quiet lot, and buyers now pay less. Which depreciation is that loss?

options.text: External obsolescence from a condition outside the owner's control
Physical deterioration from ordinary wear and aging of the house
Functional obsolescence from a floor plan buyers no longer accept
Curable deterioration the owner removes by repairing the structure

explanation: External obsolescence, also called economic obsolescence, is a loss in value from factors outside the property, such as a new freeway behind a house. The building need not be worn or poorly designed. The owner generally cannot cure it by repairing or remodeling the house, because the cause is off the lot. Physical deterioration is wear of the structure, and functional obsolescence is a design or layout defect.

distractorExplanations.b: Names physical deterioration, which is wear, damage, or aging of the improvements. The stem describes a new freeway, not a worn building.
distractorExplanations.c: Names functional obsolescence, a defect in design or layout. The house's plan is not the cause; the loss comes from the freeway outside the lot.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the loss as curable by repairing the house. Repairs do not move a freeway, so this external loss is not cured by work on the structure.

prompt: An appraiser values a fourplex by dividing net operating income by a market capitalization rate and does not deduct the mortgage payment. Which approach is that?

options.text: The cost approach, converting construction cost into a rate of return
The income approach, capitalizing net operating income into value
The sales comparison approach, because the rate was taken from sales
A gross rent multiplier, multiplying gross rent by the same rate

explanation: Direct capitalization is the income approach: value equals net operating income divided by a capitalization rate. Net operating income is income after operating expenses and before debt service, so the mortgage payment stays out. Income taxes and accounting depreciation are not operating expenses either. A rate extracted from comparable sales is evidence used inside this approach. The cost approach uses cost minus depreciation, and a gross rent multiplier uses gross rent rather than net income.

distractorExplanations.a: Names the cost approach, which adds land value to cost new and subtracts depreciation. Dividing net operating income by a capitalization rate is the income approach.
distractorExplanations.c: Mistakes a data source for the approach. Comparable sales often supply the capitalization rate, but applying that rate to net operating income is still the income approach.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes the gross rent multiplier with capitalization. A multiplier is applied to gross rent. It is not a capitalization rate multiplied by gross rent, and it does not use net operating income.

prompt: A property's net operating income is $64,000, debt service is $16,000 a year, and value is $800,000. Which capitalization rate equals that net operating income divided by that value?

options.text: A capitalization rate of 4 percent
A capitalization rate of 6 percent
A capitalization rate of 8 percent
A capitalization rate of 12.5 percent

explanation: The capitalization rate is net operating income divided by value, and debt service is not removed first. Dividing $64,000 by $800,000 gives 0.08, or 8 percent. Four percent would require income of $32,000. Six percent is what remains if the $16,000 debt service is subtracted before dividing, and that cash flow is not net operating income. Turning the division upside down, $800,000 divided by $64,000, equals 12.5, a value-to-income multiple. That multiple is not a capitalization rate, and it is not 12.5 percent.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses half the net operating income. $32,000 divided by $800,000 is 4 percent, but the income given is $64,000, and $64,000 divided by $800,000 is 8 percent.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracts the $16,000 debt service before dividing. $48,000 divided by $800,000 is 6 percent. Debt service is not deducted in arriving at the capitalization rate from net operating income.
distractorExplanations.d: Inverts the division. $800,000 divided by $64,000 equals 12.5, a value-to-income multiple. The capitalization rate is income divided by value, which is 8 percent.

prompt: An analyst wants the gross rent multiplier for a house that just sold. Which calculation produces that multiplier?

options.text: Net operating income divided by the property's sale price
The sale price divided by net operating income for the year
Gross monthly rent divided by the property's sale price
The sale price divided by the property's gross monthly rent

explanation: A gross rent multiplier is the sale price divided by gross rent, with the same rent period used on every sale. For a house, that rent is often the gross monthly rent, so the multiplier is sale price divided by gross monthly rent. Indicated value is the multiplier times gross rent. Net operating income divided by sale price is a capitalization rate, not this multiplier, and dividing rent by price inverts the multiplier.

distractorExplanations.a: Computes a capitalization rate. Net operating income divided by sale price is the cap rate. A gross rent multiplier uses sale price and gross rent, not net income.
distractorExplanations.b: Divides sale price by net operating income, which produces a value-to-net-income multiple. The gross rent multiplier uses gross rent in the denominator, not net operating income.
distractorExplanations.c: Inverts the multiplier. Gross rent divided by sale price is the reciprocal. The gross rent multiplier is sale price divided by gross rent.

prompt: Sales comparison, the cost approach, and the income approach indicate three different values for one house. How is a single opinion of value reached?

options.text: By reconciliation, weighing the indications that are more reliable here
By a straight average that counts each indication as one third
By adopting the highest indication and setting the other two aside
By adopting the lowest indication and setting the other two aside

explanation: Reconciliation is the appraiser's judgment about which value indications deserve the most weight for the property and the assignment. The final opinion is not the arithmetic mean of the three approaches, and it is not automatically the high or the low figure. For many houses the sales comparison indication is the most reliable, while an income property may lean on the income approach. The weight follows the evidence.

distractorExplanations.b: Replaces judgment with an equal split. Averaging the three indications so each is one third ignores differences in how well each approach fits the property.
distractorExplanations.c: Selects the high indication with no regard to reliability. Reconciliation does not favor the largest figure merely because it is largest.
distractorExplanations.d: Selects the low indication with no regard to reliability. A lender's caution does not make the lowest figure the reconciled value.

prompt: A vacant corner lot could support several different uses, and the appraiser has to test each one. Which set of tests is highest and best use?

options.text: Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and already the present use
Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive
Locally popular, inexpensive to construct, quick to lease, and simple to finance
Tax assessed, fully insured, free of mortgage debt, and already listed for sale

explanation: Highest and best use is the reasonably probable use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. A use that zoning forbids fails the legal test. A use that cannot physically fit the site fails the physical test. A use that does not pay its way fails financial feasibility. Among the uses that pass those tests, the one that produces the highest value is maximally productive. The present use, a cheap or popular use, and tax or insurance status are not substitutes for that test.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops maximally productive and substitutes the present use. Highest and best use can differ from the use already in place; the fourth test is the use that produces the highest value.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes popularity, cheapness, and speed for the four tests. A quick or inexpensive use is not highest and best use unless it passes those tests.
distractorExplanations.d: Lists tax, insurance, debt, and listing status. None of those is a highest-and-best-use test.

prompt: To help a seller set a list price, a salesperson studies recent sales and active listings and prepares a comparative market analysis. What is that analysis?

options.text: An appraisal, because comparable sales were used to support a price
An appraisal, because the seller will rely on it to choose a list price
Not an appraisal, and a broker price opinion is not an appraisal either
An appraisal, because the salesperson stated one recommended list price

explanation: A comparative market analysis is a licensee's pricing opinion, drawn from sales and listings, to help a client set a list price or an offer. A broker price opinion is the same kind of brokerage opinion. Under the appraisers' licensing law, an opinion a real estate licensee gives in the ordinary course of licensed brokerage is not an appraisal, and it must not be called one. Using comparable sales, putting the opinion in writing, or stating a single price does not change that.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the use of comparable sales as the definition of an appraisal. A comparative market analysis uses sales and still is not an appraisal, and it must not be labeled as one.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the client's reliance as the test. A seller may rely on a pricing opinion when choosing a list price, and that reliance does not make the opinion an appraisal.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a single stated price as the test. Recommending one list price, rather than a range, does not turn a comparative market analysis into an appraisal.

prompt: A lender orders an appraisal for a federally related home loan, and the listing salesperson is not a licensed appraiser. What may that salesperson do?

options.text: Prepare the appraisal, because a salesperson license covers this loan
Label a broker price opinion as the appraisal and send it to the lender
Ask the broker to sign the salesperson's figure and call it the appraisal
Leave the appraisal to a licensed or certified appraiser for this loan

explanation: An appraisal for a federally related loan has to be performed by a state-licensed or state-certified appraiser. A real estate salesperson license does not authorize that assignment. A broker license does not authorize it either, unless that broker is also a licensed or certified appraiser doing the appraisal. A broker price opinion or comparative market analysis cannot be retitled and delivered as the appraisal the lender ordered.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a real estate license as an appraiser license. For a federally related loan, the appraisal must come from a licensed or certified appraiser.
distractorExplanations.b: Relabels a broker price opinion as an appraisal. A price opinion is not an appraisal, and the new label does not satisfy a federally related loan.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the broker's signature as a substitute for an appraisal. Signing the salesperson's figure does not make it an appraisal for a federally related loan unless a licensed or certified appraiser actually performs the appraisal.

prompt: After both sides signed a Sacramento purchase contract, they agreed to undo the deal and return the deposit so each stood where that party stood before signing. Escrow never closed. Which remedy matches those facts?

options.text: A completed cancellation, which ends duties not yet performed and does not return the parties to their pre-contract positions.
A damages claim for breach, which keeps the contract in force and asks for money because escrow did not close.
A novation, which puts a new buyer into the contract and releases the original buyer from the duty to purchase.
A rescission, which undoes the contract and restores both parties to the positions they held before they contracted.

explanation: Rescission undoes the contract and puts both parties back where they were before they contracted. That is what these parties did: they returned the deposit and stepped back before escrow closed. A completed cancellation is different. It ends performance still to come and does not itself give back what the parties have already exchanged.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses rescission with a completed cancellation. Cancellation stops remaining duties; it does not restore both parties to their pre-contract positions.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes money damages for breach, which keeps the contract and pays for the loss. These parties undid the contract instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a novation, which substitutes a new party and releases the old duty. No new buyer took over this purchase.

prompt: Two neighbors in Fresno agree out loud on a price and a closing date for a house, shake hands, and sign nothing. The buyer asks a court to enforce the sale. What does the statute of frauds require of this deal?

options.text: A contract to purchase real property must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged before a court will enforce it.
An oral agreement to buy a house is enforceable once the parties have named both the price and the closing date.
The writing rule covers a lease longer than one year and does not apply to a contract to purchase a house.
The statute is met if a broker hears the price, because the broker can repeat the terms from memory later.

explanation: California's statute of frauds, Civil Code section 1624, requires a contract for the sale of real property to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged. These neighbors named a price and a date out loud and signed nothing, so the buyer cannot enforce that oral deal as a purchase contract.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a spoken price and closing date with a signed writing. An oral agreement to buy real property does not satisfy the statute of frauds.
distractorExplanations.c: A lease longer than one year must be written too, but that does not leave a purchase contract oral. A contract to buy real property must be in writing.
distractorExplanations.d: The broker's memory is not a writing signed by the party to be charged. Hearing the price does not satisfy the statute of frauds.

prompt: Facing a written offer, a San Diego seller crosses out the price, writes a higher price, and sends that paper back. The buyer then tries to take the original price. What is left of the original offer?

options.text: It stays open until its deadline. A price change is only a comment, so the buyer may still accept the first terms.
It is dead. The price change was a counteroffer, and a counteroffer rejects and terminates the original offer.
It became the contract when the seller read it, so the later price change came too late to affect the deal.
It survives beside the counteroffer, so the buyer may accept either the first price or the changed price.

explanation: A counteroffer rejects the original offer and replaces it with a new offer on the changed terms. Once the seller sent back a different price, the buyer's original offer was terminated. The buyer cannot accept that original price unless the seller offers it again.

distractorExplanations.a: A change in the price is not a comment that leaves the original offer open. Sending back different terms killed that offer.
distractorExplanations.c: Reading an offer does not accept it. A contract forms only if the seller accepts the same terms and that acceptance is communicated.
distractorExplanations.d: The original offer did not stay alive next to the counter. The buyer cannot choose the first price after the counter rejected it.

prompt: During the term of an Oakland exclusive right-to-sell listing, the owner finds a buyer at a picnic. No broker showed the house or wrote the offer, and the sale closes. Which fee does that listing call for?

options.text: No commission, because the owner found the buyer personally and the listing broker did not procure that buyer.
A commission only to whichever broker procured the buyer, and the owner may list the same house with several firms.
A commission to the listing broker, because the house sold during the term no matter who found the buyer.
Whatever is left above a net price the owner set, with that excess kept by the broker as the whole fee.

explanation: Under an exclusive right-to-sell listing, the listing broker earns a commission if the property sells during the term, including a sale the owner found alone. An exclusive agency listing would let the owner sell without a commission. An open listing would pay only the broker who procured the buyer.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the exclusive-agency result. Under an exclusive right-to-sell, the listing broker is still paid when the owner finds the buyer.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes an open listing. This owner signed an exclusive right-to-sell, so the listing broker is paid even though the owner found the buyer.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a net listing, which is a way of calculating the fee. It is not the exclusivity rule in an exclusive right-to-sell.

prompt: No earnest-money check accompanies a signed San Jose purchase contract in which the buyer and the seller each made a promise. The buyer fears the contract is invalid without that deposit. What is the deposit's role?

options.text: It is the down payment the lender holds until funding, and without that check the purchase contract never takes effect.
It is the consideration the law requires before any purchase contract can exist, because promises alone do not bind anyone.
It is the listing broker's commission, and the broker may take it from trust as soon as the seller accepts the offer.
It is a good-faith deposit held under the contract. The mutual promises create the contract, not the deposit.

explanation: Earnest money is a good-faith deposit. It is usually held in escrow or in a broker's trust account until closing or another release the contract allows. It does not create the contract. The buyer's promise and the seller's promise are enough consideration, so this purchase contract can be valid with no deposit at all.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses earnest money with the down payment a lender funds at closing. The deposit is not what makes the purchase contract effective.
distractorExplanations.b: Mutual promises are sufficient consideration. A missing earnest-money deposit does not keep a purchase contract from forming.
distractorExplanations.c: The deposit is not earned commission at acceptance. It stays in trust until the contract authorizes a release.

prompt: Before any purchase contract is signed, a Pasadena buyer pays a fee for the right to buy a duplex at a fixed price on or before a fixed date. The optionee has not exercised that right. What is the optionee's duty?

options.text: No duty to buy. The fee bought the right to purchase on those terms during the option period, not an obligation to buy.
A duty to complete the purchase. Paying the fee accepted a bilateral contract that requires the optionee to buy the duplex.
A duty to buy if the seller insists, because the fee left the seller free to revoke the option at any time.
A duty to close now. The option is already the purchase contract, and the fee is the purchase price of the duplex.

explanation: An option gives the optionee a right to buy on stated terms during the option period. It does not obligate the optionee to buy. The fee is consideration for that right, so the seller cannot revoke the option during the period. If the optionee never exercises it, the optionee simply does not have to purchase.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an option with a bilateral purchase contract. The option fee buys the right to purchase, not a duty to purchase.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the optionee's duty with the seller's power to revoke. Consideration keeps the option open, and the optionee still has no duty to buy.
distractorExplanations.d: The fee is the price of the option, not the price of the duplex. Until the optionee exercises, there is no duty to close.

prompt: Printed in an Irvine purchase contract is a clause that time is of the essence. The buyer misses the stated closing date and has no extension. The buyer says a short delay cannot be a breach. What does the clause do?

options.text: It adds a reasonable grace period to every date, so a late closing is still performance on time.
It makes the stated deadline material, so missing that date can be a breach because the contract says so.
It works only when a contract never mentions dates, so a written closing date deprives the clause of effect.
It removes the closing date, so either party may close whenever the funds and the deed are ready.

explanation: When the contract says time is of the essence, the dates it states are material, and missing one can be a breach. This Irvine contract says so, and the buyer has no extension. A contract that does not contain the clause does not automatically treat a short delay as a breach.

distractorExplanations.a: The clause does not add a grace period. It makes the written deadline material when the contract includes the clause.
distractorExplanations.c: The clause does its work because this contract states it. A stated closing date does not switch the clause off.
distractorExplanations.d: The clause does not erase the closing date. It is the reason that missing the date can be a breach.

prompt: A Stockton file holds three house contracts. Undue influence induced the first, fraud in the inducement induced the second, and duress by threat induced the third. No signer was adjudged incompetent or entirely without understanding, and no contract has an illegal object. What do the three contracts share?

options.text: Each is void from the start, and a later choice to ratify cannot cure the undue influence, the fraud, or the duress.
Each binds the signer as written, because a signature waives undue influence, fraud, and duress as defenses to the deal.
Each is voidable by the protected party, who may disaffirm it, and that party may later choose to ratify it.
Each is void, because undue influence, fraud, or duress counts as a court adjudication of incompetence made before signing.

explanation: Undue influence, fraud in the inducement, and duress by threat each leave a house contract voidable by the protected party. That party may disaffirm, or may later ratify once the influence, the threat, or the deception no longer controls the choice. The other side does not get the same escape. A contract is void, and cannot be ratified, when its object is illegal, when a court has adjudged the signer incompetent, or when the signer was entirely without understanding. None of those facts is present here.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses voidable with void. Undue influence, fraud in the inducement, and duress by threat let the protected party disaffirm or later ratify; they do not make the contract a nullity.
distractorExplanations.b: A signature does not waive undue influence, fraud, or duress. Those facts give the protected party a choice to avoid the contract.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses these facts with a prior adjudication of incompetence, which makes a contract void. No court had adjudged any signer incompetent, and none was entirely without understanding.

prompt: Nothing in the buyer's offer was changed when a Long Beach seller signed it and delivered that signed paper to the buyer before the offer expired. What made this an acceptance?

options.text: An unqualified assent to the offer, communicated to the buyer in the way the offer required, before the offer expired.
A change in the price or the closing date, which a real acceptance must add before any contract can be formed.
Three days of silence after the offer arrived, which accepts a purchase offer with no signature and no delivery.
Recording of the deed in the buyer's name, which is the step that accepts an offer and creates the purchase contract.

explanation: Acceptance is an unqualified agreement to the offer, communicated to the offeror as the offer requires. The seller changed nothing and delivered the signed acceptance to the buyer before the deadline, so the offer was accepted. A change in terms would have been a counteroffer. Silence is not acceptance, and signing with no communication would not have been enough.

distractorExplanations.b: A change in terms is a counteroffer, not an acceptance. Acceptance agrees to the offer without adding a new term.
distractorExplanations.c: Silence does not accept a purchase offer. The seller had to communicate an unqualified assent, which delivery of the signed paper did.
distractorExplanations.d: Recording the deed is performance after a contract exists. The purchase contract was formed when the acceptance was communicated.

prompt: Duties and a fee are set out in a Santa Rosa writing that hires one broker for a buyer. The fee applies if the buyer purchases during the term. No purchase contract has been signed. What contract is that writing?

options.text: A purchase contract that already binds the buyer to buy a house on whatever terms the brokerage form happens to contain.
An exclusive right-to-sell listing, the seller's contract that pays the broker if the property sells during the term.
A buyer-broker agreement, the employment contract that hires the broker and states how the broker is paid.
A promissory note, because the fee clause is the buyer's written promise to repay a loan secured by a house.

explanation: A buyer-broker agreement is the employment contract between the buyer and the broker. It states the broker's duties and how the broker is paid. It is not the purchase contract, and signing it does not bind the buyer to buy a particular house. A commission agreement employing a broker has to be in writing to be enforced under the statute of frauds.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the buyer-broker agreement with the purchase contract. Hiring the broker does not bind the buyer to buy a house.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses this buyer's employment contract with an exclusive right-to-sell listing. That listing is the seller's contract, and this signer is the buyer.
distractorExplanations.d: A fee clause in a brokerage agreement is not a promissory note. A note is a borrower's written promise to repay a loan.

prompt: Side by side on a Riverside loan file are a promissory note and a deed of trust against the house. The borrower wants the paper that is the contract to repay the debt. Which paper is that contract?

options.text: The deed of trust, because the security instrument is itself the borrower's promise to repay the debt on the stated terms.
The purchase agreement, because the contract to buy the house is the contract that obligates the borrower to repay the lender.
The grant deed, because passing title to the borrower is the act that creates the borrower's duty to repay the debt.
The promissory note, because it is the borrower's written contract to repay the debt under the terms stated in the note.

explanation: The promissory note is the borrower's written promise to repay the debt, and that promise is a contract. The deed of trust does not take its place. The deed of trust is the security instrument that ties the debt to the house. Swapping the two treats the lien as if it were the promise to pay.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the promissory note with the deed of trust. The deed of trust secures the debt; it is not the promise to repay.
distractorExplanations.b: The purchase agreement is the contract to buy the house. It is not the borrower's contract to repay the loan.
distractorExplanations.c: A grant deed transfers title. Delivery of title does not replace the promissory note as the contract to repay.

prompt: Loan approval is a condition in a Bakersfield purchase contract, with a stated deadline. The buyer may cancel if the loan is not approved and the condition is not waived. The buyer calls that a right to walk away for any reason at any time. What is the condition?

options.text: A use limit that remains on the house after closing and permanently restricts what the buyer may do with the property.
A contingency that must be satisfied or waived before the duty to close continues, not an open-ended right to cancel.
A stand-in for the signed purchase contract, so either party may ignore the writing and cancel the sale orally.
The seller's option to force a closing, so the buyer must complete the purchase whether or not the loan is approved.

explanation: A contingency is a condition, such as loan approval, an inspection, or an appraisal, that must be satisfied or waived before the duty to close continues. It lasts for the period the contract states. It is not a permanent right to cancel for any reason. If it fails and is not waived, the buyer may cancel under that clause, and the contract controls the deposit.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a restriction on use after closing. A loan contingency is a condition on the duty to close, not a limit on later use of the house.
distractorExplanations.c: A contingency does not replace the written purchase contract or allow an oral cancellation for any reason.
distractorExplanations.d: The contingency protects the buyer's duty to close if the loan fails and the buyer does not waive it. It is not the seller's option to force a sale.

prompt: From the sidewalk in Anaheim, a shopper reads a firm list price on a yard sign and tells the listing agent, "I accept." No purchase offer is signed. What is that list price?

options.text: An offer the shopper has accepted, so a purchase contract now exists at the price printed on the sign.
An offer that is still open, which the shopper can accept only by a signed writing under the statute of frauds.
An invitation to negotiate, not an offer, so the words "I accept" did not form a contract to buy the house.
An option the shopper now holds, so the seller must keep that price open and the shopper need not buy.

explanation: A list price on a sign is an invitation to negotiate, not an offer. The shopper cannot accept it by saying "I accept," and no purchase contract was formed. An offer is a proposal of definite terms communicated to the offeree, which is what a signed purchase offer is. There was no offer here to accept or to counter.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an invitation to negotiate with an offer. Saying "I accept" to a list price does not form a purchase contract.
distractorExplanations.b: The sign is not an offer waiting for a signature. A purchase contract must be written, but there is no offer here to accept.
distractorExplanations.d: Reading a list price does not create an option. An option needs consideration for a right to buy, and the seller is not bound.

prompt: Buried in a Modesto residential purchase contract is a liquidated-damages clause that neither party signed or initialed on its own. The buyer defaults, and the seller wants the clause enforced. What does California require before the seller can rely on it?

options.text: Nothing more. Once the parties sign the purchase contract, a liquidated-damages clause printed in it is enforceable.
A label calling the sum a penalty. The clause is enforceable only when the contract uses the word penalty.
The broker's signature on the clause. The parties' own initials do not matter if the broker has signed the form.
A separate signature or initial by each party on that clause. Without it, the seller cannot rely on the clause.

explanation: Civil Code section 1677 requires each party to sign or initial a liquidated-damages clause separately before a seller can rely on it in a contract to buy real property. Signing the Modesto purchase contract as a whole did not do that. Neither party signed or initialed this clause by itself, so the seller cannot use it as the agreed damages for the buyer's default.

distractorExplanations.a: Signing the rest of the purchase contract does not initial the liquidated-damages clause. The clause itself needs each party's separate signature or initial.
distractorExplanations.b: Calling the sum a penalty does not make the clause enforceable and does not supply the missing signature or initial.
distractorExplanations.c: The broker's signature does not replace the parties' separate signature or initial. Each buyer and seller must sign or initial the clause.

prompt: A buyer is taking a conventional loan with a small down payment, and the lender requires private mortgage insurance. That requirement is most often tied to which fact?

options.text: FHA is insuring this loan, so the charge is an FHA mortgage insurance premium rather than PMI
The VA is guaranteeing this loan, so the charge stands in place of the veteran's funding fee
The conventional loan-to-value ratio is at or below 80 percent, and that lower leverage is what triggers the premium
The conventional loan-to-value ratio is commonly above 80 percent, which is what triggers the premium

explanation: Private mortgage insurance protects a conventional lender when the borrower has thin equity. Lenders commonly require it when the loan-to-value ratio is above 80 percent. An FHA loan uses a mortgage insurance premium because FHA insures the lender, and a VA loan uses a government guarantee plus a funding fee rather than PMI.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses PMI with FHA mortgage insurance. FHA insurance is the MIP on an FHA-insured loan; PMI is the private policy used on a conventional loan.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses PMI with the VA program. A VA loan is a guarantee backed by a funding fee, and it does not use private mortgage insurance.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the equity threshold. At or below 80 percent loan-to-value, a conventional borrower usually avoids PMI; the premium is tied to higher leverage.

prompt: A borrower asks why an adjustable-rate mortgage can change while a neighbor's fixed-rate loan does not. Which statement answers that question?

options.text: The ARM rate can reset from a published index plus a set margin, and caps limit how far it moves
The ARM rate can reset from the margin alone, because the published index stays fixed for the term
The lender may reset an ARM rate whenever it chooses, because the note sets no adjustment caps
The ARM note rate stays fixed for the whole term, and a tax-escrow change is what moves the payment

explanation: An adjustable-rate note adds a margin, set at origination, to a published index. When the index moves, the rate can change at the scheduled adjustment, but periodic and lifetime caps limit that move. A fixed-rate note keeps the same interest rate for the term, even if an escrow deposit for taxes later changes the total payment.

distractorExplanations.b: Inverts the ARM formula. The margin stays constant, and movement in the index is what changes the rate at each adjustment.
distractorExplanations.c: Misses the contract limits. An ARM follows the index named in the note, and caps restrict how far the rate may rise or fall.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a fixed-rate loan whose escrow portion changes. On an ARM, the interest rate itself can reset from index plus margin.

prompt: At a California purchase, the lender prepares both a promissory note and a deed of trust. Which statement separates the two documents?

options.text: The note pledges the home as collateral, and the deed of trust is the borrower's promise to repay the debt
The note is the borrower's promise to repay the debt, and the deed of trust secures that debt with the home
The note and the deed of trust are both insurance contracts that pay the lender if the borrower later defaults
The note transfers ownership to the lender, and the deed of trust sets the brokerage commission on the sale

explanation: The promissory note is the borrower's written promise to repay the loan on the agreed rate and term. The deed of trust is the security instrument that ties that debt to the property.
