In California that security instrument also carries a power of sale, so a default can lead to a nonjudicial foreclosure. The note by itself does not pledge the home.

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the two instruments. The note is the promise to pay, and the deed of trust is what secures that promise with the property.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the loan documents with mortgage insurance. Neither the note nor the deed of trust is a policy that pays the lender on default.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the note with a conveyance and the deed of trust with a commission agreement. The note evidences the debt; the commission is a separate brokerage matter.

prompt: A California deed of trust names a trustor, a beneficiary, and a trustee on a home loan. Which description of those parties is right?

options.text: The trustor is the lender, the beneficiary is the borrower, and the trustee supplies the funds for the loan
The trustor holds the power of sale, the beneficiary stays neutral, and the trustee is the borrower on the loan
The trustor is the borrower, the beneficiary is the lender, and the trustee holds the power of sale
The trustor collects payments, the beneficiary shops the rate, and the trustee is the broker who listed the home

explanation: On a deed of trust the trustor is the borrower who pledges the property, the beneficiary is the lender who is owed the debt, and the trustee is the third party who holds the power of sale. That power of sale is what allows a nonjudicial foreclosure if the borrower defaults, so the trustee can sell without a court judgment on that path.

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps trustor and beneficiary. The trustor borrows and pledges the home; the beneficiary is the lender protected by the lien, and the lender, not the trustee, supplies the funds.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns the power of sale to the borrower and makes the trustee the borrower. The trustee, not the trustor, holds the power of sale.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes in servicing, rate shopping, and brokerage. Those jobs are not the three deed-of-trust roles of borrower, lender, and trustee.

prompt: A loan officer says the loan will be sold after closing so the lender can fund more purchases. Which market statement fits that sale?

options.text: The secondary market makes the loans to buyers, and the primary market later buys those loans from investors
The Federal Reserve runs the secondary market and sets the note rate written on each borrower's loan file
The secondary market sells private mortgage insurance, and the primary market is where those premiums are collected
The primary market makes loans to borrowers, and the secondary market buys loans so lenders get cash back

explanation: Borrowers obtain loans in the primary market from lenders and brokers. In the secondary market, investors such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy existing loans, which returns cash to the originator so more loans can be made. That purchase is liquidity. It is not origination, mortgage insurance, or a Federal Reserve rate decision.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the two markets. Origination to the borrower happens in the primary market; the secondary market buys loans after they already exist.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the secondary market with the Federal Reserve. The Fed influences rates through monetary policy; it is not the market that buys closed mortgages.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses loan sales with mortgage insurance. Private mortgage insurers cover default risk on some conventional loans; they are not the secondary market.

prompt: A homebuyer meets a mortgage loan originator at a brokerage that will not use its own money to fund the loan. What is that originator's core job?

options.text: Takes the residential application and negotiates rate or terms for pay, while a lender supplies the funds
Lends the brokerage's own money and holds that loan in portfolio until the borrower pays the balance off
Buys closed loans from retail lenders and pools those loans for sale to investors in the capital markets
Stands behind the lender the way a VA guaranty does when an eligible veteran is the borrower on the loan

explanation: A mortgage loan originator takes a residential application and negotiates rate and terms for compensation. A loan broker arranges financing between the borrower and a lender and does not fund the loan with the brokerage's own money. Lending from capital is the lender's role, and buying closed loans is the secondary market. In California, residential origination also calls for an MLO license endorsement, separate from simply arranging a sale.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes a portfolio lender, not an originator at a brokerage. The broker and the originator arrange the loan; the lender provides the funds.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes the secondary market. Originators work on the primary-market side when they take applications and place loans with lenders.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes the VA guaranty. An originator does not stand in for the Department of Veterans Affairs on a veteran's loan.

prompt: A seller wants to buy the next house before the current house has closed. Which loan is built for that short gap?

options.text: A construction loan that releases draws during the build and then converts into permanent financing
A short-term bridge loan, often used to buy the next home before the current home sale brings cash
A piggyback structure that adds a second loan so the first loan can stay at a lower loan-to-value
A rate-and-term refinance that replaces the old loan with a new long amortizing fixed-rate loan

explanation: A bridge loan, sometimes called swing financing, is short-term credit that fills the gap when a buyer must close on a new home before the sale of the current home produces cash. It is repaid when that sale closes. It is not a construction loan with draws, a piggyback used to manage leverage, or a long-term refinance.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a construction-to-permanent loan with staged draws. A bridge loan is a temporary gap loan tied to a home sale, not a build.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a piggyback, such as an 80-10-10, used to keep a first loan at lower leverage. That structure is not bridge financing.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a rate-and-term refinance. A bridge loan is short-term and is paid off when the existing home sells.

prompt: A veteran, an FHA buyer, and a conventional buyer each ask how the lender is protected. Which comparison of those loan programs is right?

options.text: VA guarantees part of an eligible loan, FHA insures the lender, and a conventional loan uses neither government backing
VA insures the lender with monthly premiums, and FHA guarantees the loan without charging the borrower any insurance
FHA and VA buy the loan after closing, while a conventional loan cannot be sold on to another investor later
A conventional loan is government-insured, and an FHA loan relies on private mortgage insurance in place of FHA coverage

explanation: A VA loan is a guarantee: the Department of Veterans Affairs stands behind part of the loan for an eligible borrower, who pays a funding fee rather than monthly mortgage insurance. An FHA loan is insurance: FHA insures the lender, and the borrower pays mortgage insurance premiums. A conventional loan has neither that guarantee nor that insurance, so high leverage is covered by private mortgage insurance instead.

distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the two programs. VA is a guarantee, not mortgage insurance, and FHA is insurance, not a VA-style guarantee.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the government programs with the secondary market. FHA and VA back loans; they do not replace investors that buy closed loans. Conventional loans are commonly sold.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the labels. A conventional loan is not FHA-insured. FHA uses its own mortgage insurance premium, not private mortgage insurance.

prompt: A borrower is offered a lower note rate if they pay discount points in cash at the loan closing. What are those points?

options.text: A prepayment penalty the lender adds if the borrower pays the entire loan off ahead of the scheduled maturity
Private mortgage insurance collected up front because this conventional loan is being made at high leverage
Prepaid interest, commonly one percent of the loan amount per point, paid to buy that lower note rate
The trustee's fee for holding a power of sale until a nonjudicial foreclosure on the home is completed

explanation: A discount point is prepaid interest. One point equals one percent of the loan amount, and paying points at closing generally buys a lower note rate over the term. That price is not a prepayment penalty, not a mortgage-insurance premium, and not a fee paid to the trustee who holds the power of sale.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses discount points with a prepayment penalty. Points are paid up front to reduce the rate; a prepayment penalty is a charge for paying the loan off early.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses points with private mortgage insurance. PMI is an insurance premium on a high-LTV conventional loan; discount points are prepaid interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses points with a trustee charge. The trustee holds the power of sale under the deed of trust; that role is not what discount points pay for.

prompt: A lender sets the maximum purchase loan from the contract price and the appraisal. Which figure is the loan-to-value ratio?

options.text: The down payment divided by the note rate, with a higher result meaning the lender has taken on less risk
The loan amount divided by value, using the lower of the purchase price and the appraised value
The monthly housing payment divided by gross income, which lenders also label as the loan-to-value ratio
The brokerage commission divided by the loan amount, quoted in the same units lenders use for discount points

explanation: Loan-to-value is the loan amount divided by the property value the lender relies on. For a purchase, lenders commonly use the lower of the purchase price and the appraised value, so the ratio shows how much of that value is being financed. A higher loan-to-value means less borrower equity and more risk, which is why conventional loans above 80 percent often require private mortgage insurance.

distractorExplanations.a: Mixes the down payment with the interest rate. Loan-to-value uses the loan amount and the property value, not the note rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Names a debt-to-income comparison, not loan-to-value. Payment compared with income is a qualifying ratio; loan-to-value compares the loan with property value.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses loan-to-value with a commission or with discount points. The ratio measures leverage on the property, not the broker's fee.

prompt: During the first years of a fully amortizing fixed-rate loan, a borrower notices most of each payment is interest. Why is that normal?

options.text: Each payment covers interest alone, and the full principal stays due as a balloon when the term ends
Each payment reduces principal alone, and the lender bills that year's interest later as a separate charge
Each payment covers interest and principal, and interest is the larger share while the balance is still high
Each payment stays interest-only until a rate adjustment, and principal starts after the first rate cap

explanation: A fully amortizing payment pays the interest then due and also reduces principal, so the balance reaches zero at the end of the term. Interest is charged on the unpaid balance, so the interest share is largest at the start and shrinks as principal is paid down. An interest-only payment does not reduce principal, and a balloon leaves a remaining balance due.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes an interest-only loan with a balloon, not full amortization. A fully amortizing payment includes principal in every installment.
distractorExplanations.b: Separates principal and interest incorrectly. Each amortizing installment pays the interest due for that period and applies the rest to principal.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes an interest-only adjustable loan. A fully amortizing fixed-rate payment reduces principal from the first installment, with no rate-cap wait.

prompt: A settlement provider offers a broker a cash fee solely for referring a borrower, and the broker will do no work on that file. Under RESPA, that fee is:

options.text: Permitted, because a lender may also pay an appraiser for an appraisal actually completed on the same loan
Permitted, because a disclosed origination fee for actually taking and processing a loan is a normal charge
Permitted, because the borrower can pay agreed discount points in exchange for a lower note rate on the loan
Prohibited, because RESPA bans giving or accepting a referral fee when no actual settlement service was performed

explanation: RESPA bars a settlement-service provider from giving or accepting a fee for a referral when no actual service was rendered for that fee. Compensation for work actually done, such as an appraisal or loan origination, is a different payment. Discount points are a loan price for a lower rate, not a referral between providers.

distractorExplanations.a: States a permitted payment for a real appraisal, which is not this offer. RESPA allows a fee for an appraisal that was performed; it bans a fee paid only for the referral.
distractorExplanations.b: States a permitted origination charge for real work. The RESPA ban in this fact pattern is the unearned referral, not a disclosed fee for originating the loan.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes discount points, which are prepaid interest for a lower rate. Points are a price term on the loan, not a referral fee for sending the borrower.

prompt: In a typical California home sale, the seller signs a grant deed to convey the fee. Which statement describes what that deed implies?

options.text: The grantor has not conveyed this estate before and has left no undisclosed encumbrance the grantor made
The grantor will defend the grantee against every title defect, including defects created by earlier owners
The grantor passes the present interest held and the deed carries no covenant about title or encumbrances
The buildings are free of physical defects at closing and the grantor will cover later damage from fire

explanation: A grant deed is the deed usually used in a California sale. From the word grant, Civil Code section 1113 implies two covenants: the grantor has not already conveyed the same estate to anyone other than the grantee, and the estate is free of encumbrances made or suffered by the grantor, other than those the deed discloses. It is not a general warranty of the whole chain of title, and it says nothing about the physical condition of the buildings.

distractorExplanations.b: This is a general warranty against defects in the chain, including those of earlier owners. A grant deed's encumbrance covenant covers encumbrances the grantor made, not every prior defect.
distractorExplanations.c: This describes a quitclaim, which passes whatever interest the grantor has and implies no covenants. A grant deed implies the two statutory covenants.
distractorExplanations.d: This confuses a title covenant with a promise about physical condition and fire. A grant deed speaks to title, not hazard coverage or building defects.

prompt: To remove a cloud on title, one co-owner signs a quitclaim deed in favor of the other co-owner. What does the grantee receive?

options.text: A warranty that the signing co-owner owns the fee and will defend every earlier defect in the chain
The covenants that this co-owner has not conveyed the estate before and has created no encumbrance on it
Title the signing co-owner may acquire after delivery, plus a covenant that the co-owner owns the fee
Whatever interest the signing co-owner holds at delivery, with no covenants about the state of title

explanation: A quitclaim transfers whatever interest the grantor has at delivery, and it makes no covenants. If the grantor has no interest, the grantee receives none. Because the deed does not grant the fee, it does not imply the grant-deed covenants and it does not pass title the grantor acquires later. It is a common instrument for clearing a possible claim, not for warranting the chain of title.

distractorExplanations.a: A defense of every earlier defect is a warranty of the chain. A quitclaim makes no covenant that the grantor owns the fee or will defend prior defects.
distractorExplanations.b: Those are the covenants implied by a California grant deed. A quitclaim carries no covenant about prior conveyances or encumbrances.
distractorExplanations.c: Title acquired later can pass under a grant of the fee. A quitclaim transfers the interest held at delivery and does not add a covenant of ownership.

prompt: After the purchase closes, the buyer holds an owner's policy of title insurance on the home. Which loss is that policy written to cover?

options.text: A covered title defect that already existed on the policy date, such as a forged deed in the chain
A kitchen fire that starts several months after the buyer has moved into the home and begun living there
A fall in market value caused by neighborhood conditions that arise after the closing of the purchase
Ordinary wear to the roof that shows up after the buyer has occupied the home for a full year

explanation: An owner's title policy indemnifies the insured against loss from covered title defects existing at the policy date, subject to the policy's exceptions and exclusions. A forged deed in the chain is that kind of existing title defect. The policy is not hazard insurance. It does not pay for a later fire, later physical wear, or a drop in market value after closing.

distractorExplanations.b: A later kitchen fire is physical damage. Hazard insurance covers that casualty. Title insurance addresses existing defects in title, not fire after the policy date.
distractorExplanations.c: A later drop in market value is not a defect in title. Title insurance does not insure neighborhood conditions or resale price after closing.
distractorExplanations.d: Roof wear that appears during occupancy is future physical damage. Title insurance does not cover the condition of the improvements.

prompt: Annual county property taxes of $3,600 are prorated in equal monthly shares on the closing statement. The seller owned the home for exactly four months of that tax year. What is the seller's tax share?

options.text: $300, one month of the $3,600 annual tax figured at $300 for each month
$1,200, four months of the $3,600 annual tax figured at $300 for each month
$2,400, eight months of the $3,600 annual tax figured at $300 for each month
$3,600, twelve months of the $3,600 annual tax figured at $300 for each month

explanation: Divide the annual tax into twelve equal months: $3,600 ÷ 12 = $300 a month. The seller owned the home for exactly four months of the tax year, so the seller's share is 4 × $300 = $1,200. The eight-month amount is the other party's share of the same year, and $3,600 is the full bill before any proration.

distractorExplanations.a: Three hundred dollars is one month of tax. The seller owned the home for four months, so a one-month charge understates the seller's share.
distractorExplanations.c: Two thousand four hundred dollars is eight months of tax, the share for the other part of the year, not the seller's four months.
distractorExplanations.d: Three thousand six hundred dollars is the entire annual bill. The seller is charged for four months of ownership, not for all twelve.

prompt: Before recording, the signed deed and the buyer's purchase funds are deposited with an escrow holder. Which description matches that holder's role at closing?

options.text: An advocate who renegotiates the price for the seller before releasing the deed or the funds
A fiduciary who may rewrite the instructions so the closing favors the buyer over the seller
A neutral stakeholder who holds the deed and funds and follows the parties' mutual instructions
A decision maker who picks a side when the buyer's and the seller's written instructions conflict

explanation: The escrow holder is a neutral stakeholder for the buyer and the seller. It holds the deed, the funds, and the other deliveries, and it closes only as the parties' mutual written instructions direct. It does not bargain for either side. If the instructions conflict, it does not choose a winner; it waits until the parties give instructions that agree.

distractorExplanations.a: Renegotiating the price for the seller would make the holder the seller's advocate. Escrow stays neutral and does not bargain for either party.
distractorExplanations.b: Rewriting the instructions to favor the buyer would take the buyer's side. Escrow follows the instructions both parties have given, rather than revising them for one side.
distractorExplanations.d: A conflict in the written instructions is not an invitation to pick a side. The holder waits for matching instructions instead of deciding which party should win.

prompt: A buyer is comparing a CLTA standard coverage policy with an ALTA extended coverage policy on the same purchase. Which comparison of those policies is accurate?

options.text: The policies cover the same title risks, and the difference is which party pays the one-time premium
The CLTA standard policy covers more off-record matters than the ALTA extended policy does
The ALTA extended policy pays for fire and later physical damage, while the CLTA policy covers title
The ALTA extended policy covers more off-record matters than the CLTA standard policy does

prompt: Two unmarried buyers take title on the same deed, in equal shares, and the deed expressly says joint tenants. At the death of one buyer, where does that buyer's share go?

options.text: It passes under the deceased buyer's will, the way a tenant-in-common share would pass at death
It passes to the surviving joint tenant by the right of survivorship stated on the deed
It is split as community property between the survivor and the heirs of the deceased buyer
It is held as sole ownership in the estate until the surviving buyer purchases that share

explanation: Joint tenancy must be stated on the deed, and this deed does that. The vesting includes a right of survivorship, so the deceased buyer's share passes to the surviving joint tenant and does not pass by will. The buyers are unmarried, so the share is not community property. Sole ownership would be title in one person alone, which is not what happens to this share at death.

distractorExplanations.a: A will can dispose of a tenant-in-common share. This deed creates a joint tenancy, so survivorship, not the will, passes the deceased buyer's share.
distractorExplanations.c: Community property is a marital vesting, and these buyers are unmarried. The deed vests joint tenancy, so the share is not divided with the heirs.
distractorExplanations.d: Sole ownership is title held by one person alone. The surviving joint tenant takes this share by survivorship, not by buying it from the estate.

prompt: Spouses buy a house during marriage with wages earned from their jobs, and the house was not a gift or an inheritance. How is that house generally characterized?

options.text: As sole ownership of the spouse whose wages paid the price, with no share left for the other spouse
As community property, so each spouse holds an undivided one-half interest in the purchased house
As joint tenancy with survivorship, even when the deed does not say that the spouses are joint tenants
As separate property of each spouse, divided by the number of hours that spouse worked during the year

explanation: Wages earned during marriage are community property, and a house bought with those wages during marriage is generally community property too. Each spouse holds an undivided one-half interest. A gift or an inheritance would be separate, but this purchase is neither. Sole ownership means one person holds title alone. Joint tenancy exists when the deed expressly creates it. Neither is the general characterization of this house.

distractorExplanations.a: Sole ownership puts title in one person alone. Wages earned during the marriage are community funds, so the house bought with them is not one spouse's sole property.
distractorExplanations.c: Joint tenancy has to be expressly declared. It is a different vesting from community property, and these facts do not create it by silence on the deed.
distractorExplanations.d: Hours worked do not turn marital wages into separate property. Earnings during marriage, and this house bought with them, are generally community property.

prompt: A longtime California owner asks how Proposition 13 limits the general property tax on a home that has not changed hands. Which statement of the limit is accurate?

Assessed value stays frozen, with no yearly factor, even after a later sale of the home, and the general rate is 1% of last year's tax bill

explanation: Proposition 13 sets a base-year value when ownership changes or new construction is completed. Until the next change in ownership or new construction, that assessed value may increase by no more than 2% a year. The general tax rate on the assessed value is capped at 1%, and voter-approved debt may be levied in addition to that 1%. A longtime owner who has not changed ownership is not reassessed to market each year.

distractorExplanations.a: This swaps the caps and reassesses the same owner every year. The annual limit on assessed value is 2%, and the general rate cap is 1% plus voter-approved debt.
distractorExplanations.b: The value is not frozen, and the 1% is not applied to last year's bill. Assessed value may rise by up to 2% a year, and a change in ownership sets a new base year.
distractorExplanations.c: The annual assessed-value cap is 2%, not 10%, and the general rate does have a cap: 1% of assessed value plus voter-approved debt.

prompt: An investor sells rental real estate held for investment and opens a like-kind exchange. Which timing rule states the federal deadlines for that exchange?

explanation: These deadlines are federal, under Internal Revenue Code section 1031. After the investor transfers the relinquished property, replacement property must be identified within 45 days, and the exchange must be completed within 180 days.
